description: Dedicated team to map abandoned but not forgotten satellites and spaceships sent into space.
summary:
On November 18, 2026, Voyager 1 will become the first spacecraft so far from Earth that a radio message takes a whole day to reach it. It launched in 1977, and it’s still out there. That got me thinking about all the other machines NASA has left behind.

I made Still Out There, a website that shows kids where NASA’s old hardware ended up and why it still matters. You can spin a globe of the Moon or Mars and click on dots to see what’s sitting at each spot, from Apollo landers to rovers that are still driving. Each one has a short card that explains what’s there now, what it discovered, and a fun fact.

The deep space section follows Voyager 1 and 2, Pioneer 10 and 11, and New Horizons. Their distance counters keep going up as you watch, and a countdown ticks toward Voyager 1’s one light-day moment.

I wanted to show that “abandoned” doesn’t mean forgotten. Some of this hardware still works, some crashed on purpose to do science, and all of it taught us something. Every location and distance comes from NASA data.
details: Still Out There is a website that teaches kids about the machines NASA has left on the Moon, on Mars and in deep space. You can spin a globe of the Moon or Mars and click on dots placed at each landing or crash site. Each dot opens a short card that explains what’s there now, what it discovered, and a fun fact. The deep space tab follows Voyager 1 and 2, Pioneer 10 and 11, and New Horizons. Their live distance counters work out each probe’s position from its distance and speed, and a countdown ticks toward Voyager 1 reaching one light-day from Earth on November 18, 2026. I built it with HTML, CSS and JavaScript, used the D3.js library to draw the globes, and took the data from NASA’s NSSDCA tables, mission pages and the JPL Horizons API. To make it creative, I used real coordinates and gave every machine one of four stories: still working, mission over, crashed on purpose, or lost on landing. That shows “abandoned” hardware often kept doing science. I kept the writing short and simple for younger readers, used both colour and words for each status so it works for colourblind users, and made sure the site works on phones, in dark mode and with a keyboard. I hope it gets students curious about space history and shows them that every mission, even a failed one, teaches us something.
